lead: A kernel must store lists of ready processes, free memory frames and open files using simple, fast data structures. Virtualization lets one machine run many isolated operating systems or containers, so the OS and hypervisor must divide CPU, memory and devices safely. Computing environments describe where that OS runs: on a desktop, a phone, a server room, a cloud data centre or a real-time controller. The same ideas of data structures and isolation appear in every environment.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for the OS as resource manager, Chapter 1.4 for dual mode, and Chapter 1.7 for kernel structure.

blocks.text: The kernel is a C program with no standard library and little spare memory. It reuses a small set of data structures. Each trades speed, memory and flexibility.
An array stores elements in contiguous memory. Index a[i] takes constant time; the size is fixed at creation. Kernels use arrays for the interrupt vector and per-CPU tables.
A linked list stores each item in a node with a pointer to the next node. Insertion and deletion are cheap after the node is found; search is O(n). Device lists and process lists use linked lists.

A stack is last-in, first-out: push adds at the top, pop removes from the top. A queue is first-in, first-out: enqueue at the tail, dequeue at the head. Function calls use stacks; ready and I/O request queues use queues.

A tree stores items in a hierarchy: each node has one parent and zero or more children. A balanced search tree gives O(log n) search, insert and delete; Linux CFS keeps runnable tasks in a red-black tree. A hash table maps a key to a bucket. Average search is O(1); collisions need chaining or open addressing. Kernel hash tables include the dentry (directory entry) cache, the inode cache and connection-tracking tables; the Linux page cache uses a radix tree (XArray) and routing entries use a trie.
A bitmap is an array of bits. Bit i is 1 if item i is used and 0 if it is free. Bitmaps track free memory frames, free disk blocks and CPU affinity masks. One 4 KB page holds 32768 bits.

Virtualization creates a virtual version of a resource: a CPU, memory, disk or whole machine. A virtual machine (VM) is a software computer with virtual CPUs (vCPUs), guest RAM and virtual devices. The hypervisor or virtual machine monitor (VMM) runs VMs and controls access to real hardware.

A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware, also called bare-metal. It boots first and starts guest operating systems. A type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host OS; the host owns hardware and the hypervisor asks it for CPU, memory and I/O. Type 1 is common in data centres; type 2 on laptops for testing.

Each VM runs its own guest kernel. The hypervisor traps privileged instructions and keeps guest memory separate. CPU overcommit is normal: the hypervisor time-slices vCPUs onto physical cores. Memory overcommit is riskier; guest pages must map to host pages, so ballooning, page sharing or swapping may be needed.
CPU ratio = (VMs × vCPUs per VM) ÷ host cores; memory ratio = (VMs × guest RAM per VM) ÷ host RAM
blocks.where: ratio > 1 means oversubscribed; ratio ≤ 1 means the host can meet the committed capacity, ignoring hypervisor overhead.

blocks.text: Containers are lighter. All containers on a host share one kernel. Linux namespaces isolate process IDs, network and mount views; control groups (cgroups) limit CPU and memory. A container starts in milliseconds and uses little memory because it does not boot a guest OS. The trade-off is weaker isolation: a kernel bug can affect every container.

Virtualization is not emulation. Emulation interprets each guest instruction in software for a different instruction set and is much slower. Virtualization runs most guest instructions directly on the CPU.
A computing environment is the hardware, OS, network and users that a program sees. The same kernel code can serve very different environments.

Traditional computing is one user on one machine: a desktop or laptop. Mobile computing adds touch input, ARM processors, battery limits and sensors; mobile OSes sandbox apps and restrict background work.

Client-server computing has a client send a request and a server reply; the web is the common example. Peer-to-peer nodes act as both clients and servers. Cloud computing rents compute, storage and network over the internet; a provider runs many VMs and containers on shared hardware.

Real-time systems must finish work before a deadline. A hard real-time miss can cause failure; a soft real-time miss only degrades quality. A distributed system is many independent computers that appear as one; it needs a network, clocks and failure handling. Distributed synchronization and file systems are in Unit 6.

An open-source OS ships source code under a licence that allows study, change and redistribution. Linux is the standard example. Open source helps debugging and teaching; support depends on the community and vendor.

figure.caption: Each extra VM raises the CPU ratio twice as fast as the memory ratio. At 8 VMs the CPU ratio is 2.0 (16 vCPUs on 8 cores) while memory sits exactly on 1.0 (32 GB of 32 GB); the flat line is ratio = 1, the point where the host is fully committed.

spec.aria: A line graph of ratio against number of VMs on an 8-core, 32 GB host. The CPU ratio line (2 vCPUs and 4 GB per VM) rises twice as fast as the memory ratio line, and a flat line marks ratio 1; at 8 VMs the CPU ratio is 2.0 and the memory ratio is 1.0.

examples.question: A cloud host has 8 cores and 32 GB RAM. It runs 8 VMs, each with 2 vCPUs and 4 GB RAM. Is the host oversubscribed in CPU or memory? Explain using virtualization.
steps: Total vCPUs = 8 VMs × 2 vCPUs per VM = 16 vCPUs.
CPU ratio = 16 vCPUs ÷ 8 host cores = 2.0. A ratio above 1 means CPU oversubscription; the hypervisor time-slices 16 vCPUs on 8 cores.
Total guest RAM = 8 VMs × 4 GB = 32 GB.
Memory ratio = 32 GB ÷ 32 GB = 1.0. The host is fully committed but not oversubscribed; ratio 1.0 means guest RAM equals host RAM, before hypervisor overhead.
If all VMs touch all pages, the host has no spare frame. Any hypervisor overhead would force swapping or ballooning, so real deployments keep some headroom.
Answer: CPU is oversubscribed 2:1; memory is exactly committed with ratio 1.0, not oversubscribed.
examples.answer: CPU is oversubscribed by a factor of 2.0; memory is exactly committed at 32 GB and is not oversubscribed.

traps: Virtualization is not emulation. Emulation interprets instructions for a different instruction set; virtualization runs most same-ISA instructions directly.
Type 1 runs on bare hardware; type 2 runs on a host OS. Swapping these names loses marks.
Container = shared host kernel, no guest kernel.
CPU overcommit is common and usually safe; memory overcommit can cause host swapping and unpredictable latency. Ratio > 1 means oversubscribed, not broken.
A bitmap uses one bit per item, not one byte. 1 byte = 8 bits, so multiply bytes by 8 to get bitmap capacity.

quiz.q: Name four kernel data structures and one kernel use of each.
quiz.a: Array: interrupt vector. Linked list: device list. Queue: ready queue. Bitmap: free frames.

quiz.q: Why does a container start faster than a VM?
quiz.a: It shares the host kernel and does not boot a guest OS, so it avoids kernel boot and device initialisation.

quiz.q: A host has 16 cores and 64 GB RAM. It runs 10 VMs, each with 4 vCPUs and 8 GB RAM. Find CPU ratio and memory ratio. Is either oversubscribed?
quiz.a: Total vCPUs = 10 × 4 = 40; CPU ratio = 40 ÷ 16 = 2.5. Total RAM = 10 × 8 = 80 GB; memory ratio = 80 ÷ 64 = 1.25. Both are above 1, so both are oversubscribed.

quiz.q: Where does a guest disk write travel under a type 2 hypervisor?
quiz.a: Guest kernel → virtual disk in hypervisor → host OS file or block layer → host driver → hardware. The host OS layer adds overhead but isolates the guest.

quiz.q: What does a bitmap store, and how many frames can one 4 KB page track if one bit tracks one frame?
quiz.a: One bit per item. 4 KB = 4096 bytes = 32768 bits, so 32768 frames.

quiz.q: Why is memory overcommit riskier than CPU overcommit?
quiz.a: A vCPU can be time-sliced; a guest page still needs a physical frame. If guests touch more pages than host RAM, the host must swap or balloon, causing long delays and possible failure.

beyond: Not for the exam. Cloud providers use microVMs such as Firecracker to combine VM isolation with container-like startup times. Confidential computing encrypts guest memory so the host cannot read it. Kernel data structures appear in eBPF maps and io_uring queues. Search for 'Linux namespaces cgroups', 'type 1 hypervisor' and 'microVM'.
